raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old Caucasian girl with history of common variable immunodeficiency presented with a 6-day history of nonpruritic, photo-distributed rash on face, arms, and legs associated with swelling of arms. The rash started after she was playing in the farm on a sunny day for a few hours. There was no history of fever. She had burning sensation in her eyes without drainage or blurring of her vision for a few hours prior to admission. She also had dryness with redness and early blistering lesions on her lips. She has no history of recent sick contacts.
She was diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency at the age of 3 years following recurrent hospitalizations for ear infections and bacterial pneumonia. She receives monthly intravenous immunoglobulin therapy. In the last 5 months, she developed recurrent episodes of cough and hemoptysis. Chest computed tomography (CT) scan showed tree in bud appearance and bronchoalveolar lavage fungal culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus. She was given oral voriconazole 200 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, which was then increased to 300 mg twice daily, 10 days prior to presentation, due to subtherapeutic serum voriconazole level. Her other medications at the time of admission were the following: Vynase (Lesdexapmphetamine), 50 mg once a day, and Seroquel (Quetiapine), which was stopped 10 days prior to presentation in view of theoretical risk of QT prolongation due to drug interaction with voriconazole.
Her physical examination revealed a well-built, well-nourished teenager. She was alert but in moderate distress due to burning sensation of the arms and face. Her vital signs showed a temperature of 36.7 C, heart rate 65/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and blood pressure of 117/69 mm Hg. She had an erythematous rash on the face and both arms up to midarm level with swelling of both arms. The rash was also present on the neck and lower extremities. The skin was erythematous and shiny with tenderness to touch and pressure in all photo-distribution areas but was sparing the truncal area, buttocks, and the genital area. She also had cracked lips with mild bleeding without swelling or oral ulcers (Figure 1). The rest of the physical examination was normal.
Laboratory investigations at admission were as follows: white blood cells 3900/mm3 (neutrophils 74%, lymphocytes 16%, monocytes 8%, eosinophil 2%), hemoglobin 13.9 gm/dL, hematocrit 41.6%, platelets 196 000/mm3. Serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, bilirubin total 0.7 mg/dL, bilirubin direct <0.1 mg/dL, alanine aminotrasferase 17 U/L, aspartate aminotrasferase 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 93 U/L. Blood culture was negative. Voriconazole level by high-performance liquid chromatography was 2.5 microg/mL (therapeutic range being 2-6 microg/mL). Serum parvovirus B-19, Mycoplasma, and herpes simplex IgM levels were all negative.
She was admitted to the burn unit and was treated with intravenous fluid hydration and frequent Vaseline dressings to the affected areas for 2 days. This was followed by topical triamcinolone (0.1%) cream. Voriconazole was discontinued at the time of presentation. A skin biopsy showed mild vacuolar interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes and superficial vessel involvement consistent with photosensitivity reactions. The rash gradually improved. The patient also reported improvement in tenderness and swelling of the extremities. Lip sores also improved in few days. She was instructed to minimize sun exposure and always use sun screens. The symptoms and skin findings resolved after 10 days. She completed a 6-week course of antifungal therapy for pulmonary aspergillosis with intravenous micafungin.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old Caucasian girl with common variable immunodeficiency on voriconazole for pulmonary aspergillosis presented with a 6-day history of a painful, nonpruritic photo-distributed rash on her face, neck, arms, and legs, arm swelling, burning eyes, and cracked bleeding lips.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Five months prior to admission, the patient developed recurrent cough and hemoptysis and was diagnosed with pulmonary Aspergillus fumigatus infection; she was started on oral voriconazole 200 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, which was increased to 300 mg twice daily 10 days prior to admission due to a subtherapeutic serum trough level. Six days before admission, after playing outdoors on a sunny farm for a few hours, she developed a painful, burning, nonpruritic erythematous rash across sun-exposed areas (face, neck, forearms/arms, and legs) with bilateral arm swelling, cracked bleeding lips with early blistering, and a burning sensation in her eyes.
subjective.past_medical_history: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) diagnosed at age 3 following recurrent otitis media and bacterial pneumonias, maintained on monthly IVIG; pulmonary Aspergillus fumigatus infection diagnosed 5 months prior. Concomitant medications: lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) 50 mg daily, voriconazole 300 mg twice daily (quetiapine stopped 10 days prior to avoid QT prolongation).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful burning photosensitive rash, bilateral arm edema, cracked bleeding lips, and ocular burning; negative for fever, pruritus, ocular discharge, visual blurring, or recent sick contacts.

objective.physical_examination: Well-built, alert teenager in moderate distress from skin burning; temperature 36.7 C, heart rate 65 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and blood pressure 117/69 mmHg. Skin exam showed a shiny, tender, erythematous rash strictly localized to photo-distributed areas (face, neck, bilateral upper limbs to mid-arm with arm edema, and lower extremities), completely sparing the trunk, buttocks, and genital area, along with cracked, mildly bleeding lips without intraoral ulcers.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs were normal: WBC 3,900/mm3 (74% neutrophils, 16% lymphocytes, 8% monocytes, 2% eosinophils), hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, hematocrit 41.6%, platelets 196,000/mm3, normal electrolytes, BUN 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin <0.1 mg/dL, ALT 17 U/L, AST 28 U/L, and ALP 93 U/L. Blood cultures and serum IgM serologies for parvovirus B19, Mycoplasma, and HSV were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Prior workup 5 months earlier showed tree-in-bud opacities on chest CT and Aspergillus fumigatus growth on bronchoalveolar lavage fungal culture. At current admission, serum voriconazole trough concentration by HPLC was 2.5 ug/mL (therapeutic range 2-6 ug/mL). Skin biopsy demonstrated mild vacuolar interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes and superficial vascular involvement consistent with an acute phototoxic drug reaction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Voriconazole-induced acute phototoxic dermatitis and cheilitis following sun exposure 4 days after a voriconazole dose escalation (from 200 mg to 300 mg twice daily) for pulmonary Aspergillus fumigatus infection in an adolescent with common variable immunodeficiency, confirmed by characteristic photo-distribution, therapeutic HPLC voriconazole level (2.5 ug/mL), and skin biopsy showing vacuolar interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes. Managed in the burn unit by immediately discontinuing voriconazole, applying Vaseline dressings and topical 0.1% triamcinolone cream with IV hydration, and completing her 6-week pulmonary aspergillosis regimen with intravenous micafungin; skin and lip lesions completely resolved within 10 days.
